#Text=Methinks the time runs very fleet.
#Text=All my joys to this are folly,
#Text= Naught so sweet as melancholy.
#Text=When I lie waking all alone,
#Text= Recounting what I have ill done,
#Text= My thoughts on me then tyrannise,
#Text= Fear and sorrow me surprise,
#Text= Whether I tarry still or go,
#Text= Methinks the time moves very slow.
#Text=All my griefs to this are jolly,
#Text= Naught so mad as melancholy.
#Text=When to myself I act and smile,
#Text= With pleasing thoughts the time beguile,
#Text= By a brook side or wood so green,
#Text= Unheard, unsought for, or unseen,
#Text= A thousand pleasures do me bless,
#Text= And crown my soul with happiness.
#Text=All my joys besides are folly,
#Text= None so sweet as melancholy.
#Text=When I lie, sit, or walk alone,
#Text=I sigh, I grieve, making great moan,
#Text= In a dark grove, or irksome den,
#Text= With discontents and Furies then,
#Text= A thousand miseries at once
#Text= Mine heavy heart and soul ensconce,
#Text= All my griefs to this are jolly,
#Text= None so sour as melancholy.
#Text=Methinks I hear, methinks I see,
#Text= Sweet music, wondrous melody,
#Text= Towns, palaces, and cities fine;
#Text= Here now, then there; the world is mine,
#Text= Rare beauties, gallant ladies shine,
#Text= Whate  '  er is lovely or divine.
#Text=All other joys to this are folly,
#Text= None so sweet as melancholy.
#Text=Methinks I hear, methinks I see
#Text= Ghosts, goblins, fiends; my phantasy
#Text= Presents a thousand ugly shapes,
#Text= Headless bears, black men, and apes,
#Text= Doleful outcries, and fearful sights,
#Text=My sad and dismal soul affrights.
#Text=All my griefs to this are jolly,
#Text= None so damn  '  d as melancholy.
#Text=Methinks I court, methinks I kiss,
#Text= Methinks I now embrace my mistress.
#Text=O blessed days, O sweet content,
#Text= In Paradise my time is spent.
#Text=Such thoughts may still my fancy move,
#Text= So may I ever be in love.
#Text=All my joys to this are folly,
#Text= Naught so sweet as melancholy.
#Text=When I recount love  '  s many frights,
#Text= My sighs and tears, my waking nights,
#Text= My jealous fits; O mine hard fate
#Text= I now repent, but   '  tis too late.
#Text=No torment is so bad as love,
#Text= So bitter to my soul can prove.
#Text=All my griefs to this are jolly,
#Text= Naught so harsh as melancholy.
#Text=Friends and companions get you gone,
#Text=
#Text= _Taste_.]
#Text=Taste, a necessary sense, "which perceives all savours by the
#Text= tongue and palate, and that by means of a thin spittle, or watery juice."
#Text=His organ is the tongue with his tasting nerves; the medium, a watery
#Text= juice; the object, taste, or savour, which is a quality in the juice,
#Text= arising from the mixture of things tasted.
#Text=Some make eight species or kinds
#Text= of savour, bitter, sweet, sharp, salt, &c., all which sick men (as in an
#Text= ague) cannot discern, by reason of their organs misaffected.
#Text=_Touching_.]
#Text=Touch, the last of the senses, and most ignoble, yet of as
#Text= great necessity as the other, and of as much pleasure.
#Text=This sense is
#Text= exquisite in men, and by his nerves dispersed all over the body, perceives
#Text= any tactile quality.
#Text=His organ the nerves; his object those first
#Text= qualities, hot, dry, moist, cold; and those that follow them, hard, soft,
#Text= thick, thin, &c.
#Text=Many delightsome questions are moved by philosophers about
#Text= these five senses; their organs, objects, mediums, which for brevity I
#Text= omit.
#Text=SUBSECT.
#Text=VII.
#Text=--_Of the Inward Senses._
#Text=_Venter Deus_: They wear "their brains in their bellies, and their guts in
#Text= their heads," as [1412]Agrippa taxed some parasites of his time, rushing on
#Text= their own destruction, as if a man should run upon the point of a sword,
#Text= _usque dum rumpantur comedunt_, "They eat till they burst:" [1413]All day,
#Text= all night, let the physician say what he will, imminent danger, and feral
#Text= diseases are now ready to seize upon them, that will eat till they vomit,
#Text= _Edunt ut vomant, vomut ut edant_, saith Seneca; which Dion relates of
#Text= Vitellius, _Solo transitu ciborum nutriri judicatus_: His meat did pass
#Text= through and away, or till they burst again. [1414]_Strage animantium
#Text= ventrem onerant_, and rake over all the world, as so many [1415]slaves,
#Text= belly-gods, and land-serpents, _Et totus orbis ventri nimis angustus_, the
#Text= whole world cannot satisfy their appetite. [1416]"Sea, land, rivers, lakes,
#Text= &c., may not give content to their raging guts."
#Text=To make up the mess, what
#Text= immoderate drinking in every place?
#Text=_Senem potum pota trahebat anus_, how
#Text= they flock to the tavern: as if they were _fruges consumere nati_, born to
#Text= no other end but to eat and drink, like Offellius Bibulus, that famous
#Text= Roman parasite, _Qui dum vixit, aut bibit aut minxit_; as so many casks to
#Text= hold wine, yea worse than a cask, that mars wine, and itself is not marred
#Text= by it, yet these are brave men, Silenus Ebrius was no braver.
#Text=_Et quae
#Text= fuerunt vitia, mores sunt_:   '  tis now the fashion of our times, an honour:
#Text=used to them it makes bad meats wholesome, and unseasonable times to cause
#Text= no disorder.
#Text=Cider and perry are windy drinks, so are all fruits windy in
#Text= themselves, cold most part, yet in some shires of [1440]England, Normandy
#Text= in France, Guipuscoa in Spain,   '  tis their common drink, and they are no
#Text= whit offended with it.
#Text=In Spain, Italy, and Africa, they live most on
#Text= roots, raw herbs, camel  '  s [1441]milk, and it agrees well with them: which
#Text= to a stranger will cause much grievance.
#Text=In Wales, _lacticiniis vescuntur_,
#Text= as Humphrey Llwyd confesseth, a Cambro-Briton himself, in his elegant
#Text= epistle to Abraham Ortelius, they live most on white meats: in Holland on
#Text= fish, roots, [1442]butter; and so at this day in Greece, as [1443]Bellonius
#Text= observes, they had much rather feed on fish than flesh.
#Text=With us, _Maxima
#Text= pars victus in carne consistit_, we feed on flesh most part, saith
#Text= [1444]Polydore Virgil, as all northern countries do; and it would be very
#Text= offensive to us to live after their diet, or they to live after ours.
#Text=We
#Text= drink beer, they wine; they use oil, we butter; we in the north are
#Text= [1445]great eaters; they most sparing in those hotter countries; and yet
#Text= they and we following our own customs are well pleased.
#Text=An Ethiopian of old
#Text= seeing an European eat bread, wondered, _quomodo stercoribus vescentes
#Text= viverimus_, how we could eat such kind of meats: so much differed his
#Text= countrymen from ours in diet, that as mine [1446]author infers, _si quis
#Text=illorum victum apud nos aemulari vellet_; if any man should so feed with
#Text= us, it would be all one to nourish, as Cicuta, Aconitum, or Hellebore
#Text= itself.
#Text=At this day in China the common people live in a manner altogether
#Text= on roots and herbs, and to the wealthiest, horse, ass, mule, dogs,
#Text= cat-flesh, is as delightsome as the rest, so [1447]Mat.
#Text=Riccius the Jesuit
#Text= relates, who lived many years amongst them.
#Text=The Tartars eat raw meat, and
#Text= most commonly [1448]horse-flesh, drink milk and blood, as the nomades of
#Text= old.
#Text=_Et lac concretum cum sanguine potat equino_.
#Text=They scoff at our
#Text= Europeans for eating bread, which they call tops of weeds, and horse meat,
#Text= not fit for men; and yet Scaliger accounts them a sound and witty nation,
#Text= living a hundred years; even in the civilest country of them they do thus,
#Text= as Benedict the Jesuit observed in his travels, from the great Mogul  '  s
#Text= Court by land to Pekin, which Riccius contends to be the same with Cambulu
#Text= in Cataia.
#Text=In Scandia their bread is usually dried fish, and so likewise in
#Text= the Shetland Isles; and their other fare, as in Iceland, saith
#Text= [1449]Dithmarus Bleskenius, butter, cheese, and fish; their drink water,
#Text= their lodging on the ground.
#Text=In America in many places their bread is
#Text= roots, their meat palmettos, pinas, potatoes, &c., and such fruits.
#Text=There
#Text= be of them too that familiarly drink [1450]salt seawater all their lives,
#Text= eat [1451]raw meat, grass, and that with delight.
#Text=With some, fish,
#Text=serpents, spiders: and in divers places they [1452]eat man  '  s flesh, raw and
#Text= roasted, even the Emperor [1453]Montezuma himself.
#Text=In some coasts, again,
#Text= [1454]one tree yields them cocoanuts, meat and drink, fire, fuel, apparel;
#Text= with his leaves, oil, vinegar, cover for houses, &c., and yet these men
#Text= going naked, feeding coarse, live commonly a hundred years, are seldom or
#Text= never sick; all which diet our physicians forbid.
#Text=In Westphalia they feed
#Text= most part on fat meats and worts, knuckle deep, and call it [1455]_cerebrum
#Text= Iovis_: in the Low Countries with roots, in Italy frogs and snails are
#Text= used.
#Text=The Turks, saith Busbequius, delight most in fried meats.
#Text=In Muscovy,
#Text= garlic and onions are ordinary meat and sauce, which would be pernicious to
#Text= such as are unaccustomed to them, delightsome to others; and all is
#Text= [1456]because they have been brought up unto it.
#Text=Husbandmen, and such as
#Text= labour, can eat fat bacon, salt gross meat, hard cheese, &c., (_O dura
#Text= messorum illa_), coarse bread at all times, go to bed and labour upon a
#Text= full stomach, which to some idle persons would be present death, and is
#Text= against the rules of physic, so that custom is all in all.
#Text=Our travellers
#Text= find this by common experience when they come in far countries, and use
#Text= their diet, they are suddenly offended, [1457]as our Hollanders and
#Text= Englishmen when they touch upon the coasts of Africa, those Indian capes
#Text= and islands, are commonly molested with calentures, fluxes, and much
#Text=distempered by reason of their fruits. [1458]_Peregrina, etsi suavia solent
#Text= vescentibus perturbationes insignes adferre_, strange meats, though
#Text= pleasant, cause notable alterations and distempers.
#Text=On the other side, use
#Text= or custom mitigates or makes all good again.
#Text=Mithridates by often use,
#Text= which Pliny wonders at, was able to drink poison; and a maid, as Curtius
#Text= records, sent to Alexander from King Porus, was brought up with poison from
#Text= her infancy.
#Text=The Turks, saith Bellonius, lib. 3. c. 15, eat opium
#Text= familiarly, a dram at once, which we dare not take in grains. [1459]Garcias
#Text= ab Horto writes of one whom he saw at Goa in the East Indies, that took ten
#Text= drams of opium in three days; and yet _consulto loquebatur_, spake
#Text= understandingly, so much can custom do. [1460] Theophrastus speaks of a
#Text= shepherd that could eat hellebore in substance.
#Text=And therefore Cardan
#Text= concludes out of Galen, _Consuetudinem utcunque ferendam, nisi valde
#Text= malam_.
#Text=Custom is howsoever to be kept, except it be extremely bad: he
#Text= adviseth all men to keep their old customs, and that by the authority of
#Text= [1461]Hippocrates himself, _Dandum aliquid tempori, aetati regioni,
#Text= consuetudini_, and therefore to [1462]continue as they began, be it diet,
#Text= bath, exercise, &c., or whatsoever else.
#Text=Another exception is delight, or appetite, to such and such meats: though
#Text=they be hard of digestion, melancholy; yet as Fuchsius excepts, _cap. 6.
#Text=lib. 2.
#Text=Instit. sect. 2_, [1463]"The stomach doth readily digest, and
#Text= willingly entertain such meats we love most, and are pleasing to us, abhors
#Text= on the other side such as we distaste."
#Text=Which Hippocrates confirms,
#Text= _Aphoris. 2. 38._ Some cannot endure cheese, out of a secret antipathy; or
#Text= to see a roasted duck, which to others is a [1464]delightsome meat.
#Text=The last exception is necessity, poverty, want, hunger, which drives men
#Text= many times to do that which otherwise they are loath, cannot endure, and
#Text= thankfully to accept of it: as beverage in ships, and in sieges of great
#Text= cities, to feed on dogs, cats, rats, and men themselves.
#Text=Three outlaws in
#Text= [1465]Hector Boethius, being driven to their shifts, did eat raw flesh, and
#Text= flesh of such fowl as they could catch, in one of the Hebrides for some few
#Text= months.
#Text=These things do mitigate or disannul that which hath been said of
#Text= melancholy meats, and make it more tolerable; but to such as are wealthy,
#Text= live plenteously, at ease, may take their choice, and refrain if they will,
#Text= these viands are to be forborne, if they be inclined to, or suspect
#Text= melancholy, as they tender their healths: Otherwise if they be intemperate,
#Text= or disordered in their diet, at their peril be it.
#Text=_Qui monet amat, Ave et
#Text= cave_.
#Text=[2901]eggs are justified as a nutritive wholesome meat, butter and oil may
#Text= pass, but with some limitation; so [2902]Crato confines it, and "to some
#Text= men sparingly at set times, or in sauce," and so sugar and honey are
#Text= approved. [2903]All sharp and sour sauces must be avoided, and spices, or
#Text= at least seldom used: and so saffron sometimes in broth may be tolerated;
#Text= but these things may be more freely used, as the temperature of the party
#Text= is hot or cold, or as he shall find inconvenience by them.
#Text=The thinnest,
#Text= whitest, smallest wine is best, not thick, nor strong; and so of beer, the
#Text= middling is fittest.
#Text=Bread of good wheat, pure, well purged from the bran
#Text= is preferred; Laurentius, _cap. 8._ would have it kneaded with rain water,
#Text= if it may be gotten.
#Text=_Water_.]
#Text=Pure, thin, light water by all means use, of good smell and
#Text= taste, like to the air in sight, such as is soon hot, soon cold, and which
#Text= Hippocrates so much approves, if at least it may be had.
#Text=Rain water is
#Text= purest, so that it fall not down in great drops, and be used forthwith, for
#Text= it quickly putrefies.
#Text=Next to it fountain water that riseth in the east,
#Text= and runneth eastward, from a quick running spring, from flinty, chalky,
#Text= gravelly grounds: and the longer a river runneth, it is commonly the
#Text= purest, though many springs do yield the best water at their fountains.
#Text=The
#Text=Gillius, in his accurate description of Constantinople, speaks of an old
#Text= cistern which he went down to see, 336 feet long, 180 feet broad, built of
#Text= marble, covered over with arch-work, and sustained by 336 pillars, 12 feet
#Text= asunder, and in eleven rows, to contain sweet water.
#Text=Infinite cost in
#Text= channels and cisterns, from Nilus to Alexandria, hath been formerly
#Text= bestowed, to the admiration of these times; [2913]their cisterns so
#Text= curiously cemented and composed, that a beholder would take them to be all
#Text= of one stone: when the foundation is laid, and cistern made, their house is
#Text= half built.
#Text=That Segovian aqueduct in Spain, is much wondered at in these
#Text= days, [2914]upon three rows of pillars, one above another, conveying sweet
#Text= water to every house: but each city almost is full of such aqueducts.
#Text=Amongst the rest [2915]he is eternally to be commended, that brought that
#Text= new stream to the north side of London at his own charge: and Mr.
#Text=Otho
#Text= Nicholson, founder of our waterworks and elegant conduit in Oxford.
#Text=So much
#Text= have all times attributed to this element, to be conveniently provided of
#Text= it: although Galen hath taken exceptions at such waters, which run through
#Text= leaden pipes, _ob cerussam quae in iis generatur_, for that unctuous
#Text= ceruse, which causeth dysenteries and fluxes; [2916]yet as Alsarius Crucius
#Text= of Genna well answers, it is opposite to common experience.
#Text=If that were
#Text= true, most of our Italian cities, Montpelier in France, with infinite
#Text=others, would find this inconvenience, but there is no such matter.
#Text=For
#Text= private families, in what sort they should furnish themselves, let them
#Text= consult with P.
#Text=Crescentius, _de Agric. l. 1. c. 4_, Pamphilius Hirelacus,
#Text= and the rest.
#Text=Amongst fishes, those are most allowed of, that live in gravelly or sandy
#Text= waters, pikes, perch, trout, gudgeon, smelts, flounders, &c.
#Text=Hippolitus
#Text= Salvianus takes exception at carp; but I dare boldly say with [2917]
#Text= Dubravius, it is an excellent meat, if it come not from [2918]muddy pools,
#Text= that it retain not an unsavoury taste.
#Text=Erinacius Marinus is much commended
#Text= by Oribatius, Aetius, and most of our late writers
#Text=.
#Text=[2919]Crato, _consil. 21. lib. 2._ censures all manner of fruits, as
#Text= subject to putrefaction, yet tolerable at sometimes, after meals, at second
#Text= course, they keep down vapours, and have their use.
#Text=Sweet fruits are best,
#Text= as sweet cherries, plums, sweet apples, pearmains, and pippins, which
#Text= Laurentius extols, as having a peculiar property against this disease, and
#Text= Plater magnifies, _omnibus modis appropriata conveniunt_, but they must be
#Text= corrected for their windiness: ripe grapes are good, and raisins of the
#Text= sun, musk-melons well corrected, and sparingly used.
#Text=Figs are allowed, and
#Text=in the market at once, it is in so great request with them.
#Text=SUBSECT.
#Text=II.
#Text=--_Diet rectified in quantity_.
#Text=Man alone, saith [2926]Cardan, eats and drinks without appetite, and useth
#Text= all his pleasure without necessity, _animae vitio_, and thence come many
#Text= inconveniences unto him.
#Text=For there is no meat whatsoever, though otherwise
#Text= wholesome and good, but if unseasonably taken, or immoderately used, more
#Text= than the stomach can well bear, it will engender crudity, and do much harm.
#Text=Therefore [2927]Crato adviseth his patient to eat but twice a day, and that
#Text= at his set meals, by no means to eat without an appetite, or upon a full
#Text= stomach, and to put seven hours  '   difference between dinner and supper.
#Text=Which rule if we did observe in our colleges, it would be much better for
#Text= our healths: but custom, that tyrant, so prevails, that contrary to all
#Text= good order and rules of physic, we scarce admit of five.
#Text=If after seven
#Text= hours  '   tarrying he shall have no stomach, let him defer his meal, or eat
#Text= very little at his ordinary time of repast.
#Text=This very counsel was given by
#Text= Prosper Calenus to Cardinal Caesius, labouring of this disease; and [2928]
#Text= Platerus prescribes it to a patient of his, to be most severely kept.
#Text=Guianerius admits of three meals a day, but Montanus, _consil. 23. pro.
#Text=Ab.
#Text=Italo_, ties him precisely to two.
#Text=And as he must not eat overmuch, so he
#Text= may not absolutely fast; for as Celsus contends, _lib. 1.
#Text=Jacchinus 15. in
#Text= 9.
#Text=Rhasis_, [2929]repletion and inanition may both do harm in two contrary
#Text= extremes.
#Text=Moreover, that which he doth eat, must be well [2930]chewed, and
#Text= not hastily gobbled, for that causeth crudity and wind; and by all means to
#Text= eat no more than he can well digest.
#Text="Some think" (saith [2931]
#Text= Trincavelius, _lib. 11. cap. 29. de curand. part. hum._) "the more they eat
#Text= the more they nourish themselves:" eat and live, as the proverb is, "not
#Text= knowing that only repairs man, which is well concocted, not that which is
#Text= devoured."
#Text=Melancholy men most part have good [2932]appetites, but ill
#Text= digestion, and for that cause they must be sure to rise with an appetite;
#Text= and that which Socrates and Disarius the physicians in [2933]Macrobius so
#Text= much require, St.
#Text=Hierom enjoins Rusticus to eat and drink no more than,
#Text= will [2934]satisfy hunger and thirst. [2935]Lessius, the Jesuit, holds
#Text= twelve, thirteen, or fourteen ounces, or in our northern countries, sixteen
#Text= at most, (for all students, weaklings, and such as lead an idle sedentary
#Text= life) of meat, bread, &c., a fit proportion for a whole day, and as much or
#Text= little more of drink.
#Text=Nothing pesters the body and mind sooner than to be
#Text= still fed, to eat and ingurgitate beyond all measure, as many do. [2936]
#Text=will transform a beast to a man again, so will it make a man a God.
#Text=To
#Text= preserve thine honour, health, and to avoid therefore all those inflations,
#Text= torments, obstructions, crudities, and diseases that come by a full diet,
#Text= the best way is to [2942]feed sparingly of one or two dishes at most, to
#Text= have _ventrem bene moratum_, as Seneca calls it, [2943]"to choose one of
#Text= many, and to feed on that alone," as Crato adviseth his patient.
#Text=The same
#Text= counsel [2944]Prosper Calenus gives to Cardinal Caesius, to use a moderate
#Text= and simple diet: and though his table be jovially furnished by reason of
#Text= his state and guests, yet for his own part to single out some one savoury
#Text= dish and feed on it.
#Text=The same is inculcated by [2945]Crato, _consil. 9. l.
#Text= 2._ to a noble personage affected with this grievance, he would have his
#Text= highness to dine or sup alone, without all his honourable attendance and
#Text= courtly company, with a private friend or so, [2946]a dish or two, a cup of
#Text= Rhenish wine, &c.
#Text=Montanus, _consil. 24._ for a noble matron enjoins her
#Text= one dish, and by no means to drink between meals.
#Text=The like, _consil. 229._
#Text= or not to eat till he be an hungry, which rule Berengarius did most
#Text= strictly observe, as Hilbertus, _Cenomecensis Episc._ writes in his life,
#Text=
#Text= ------"cui non fuit unquam
#Text= Ante sitim potus, nec cibus ante famem,"
#Text=
#Text= and which all temperate men do constantly keep.
#Text=It is a frequent solemnity
#Text= still used with us, when friends meet, to go to the alehouse or tavern,
#Text= they are not sociable otherwise: and if they visit one another  '  s houses,
#Text= they must both eat and drink.
#Text=I reprehend it not moderately used; but to
#Text= some men nothing can be more offensive; they had better, I speak it with
#Text= Saint [2947]Ambrose, pour so much water in their shoes.
#Text=It much avails likewise to keep good order in our diet, [2948]"to eat
#Text= liquid things first, broths, fish, and such meats as are sooner corrupted
#Text= in the stomach; harder meats of digestion must come last."
#Text=Crato would have
#Text= the supper less than the dinner, which Cardan, _Contradict. lib. 1. tract.
#Text= 5. contradict. 18._ disallows, and that by the authority of Galen. _7. art.
#Text=curat. cap. 6._ and for four reasons he will have the supper biggest: I
#Text= have read many treatises to this purpose, I know not how it may concern
#Text= some few sick men, but for my part generally for all, I should subscribe to
#Text= that custom of the Romans, to make a sparing dinner, and a liberal supper;
#Text= all their preparation and invitation was still at supper, no mention of
#Text= dinner.
#Text=Many reasons I could give, but when all is said _pro_ and _con_,
#Text= [2949]Cardan  '  s rule is best, to keep that we are accustomed unto, though it
#Text=wind and windows, that he holds it alone sufficient to make a man sick or
#Text= well; to alter body and mind. [3185]"A clear air cheers up the spirits,
#Text= exhilarates the mind; a thick, black, misty, tempestuous, contracts,
#Text= overthrows."
#Text=Great heed is therefore to be taken at what times we walk, how
#Text= we place our windows, lights, and houses, how we let in or exclude this
#Text= ambient air.
#Text=The Egyptians, to avoid immoderate heat, make their windows on
#Text= the top of the house like chimneys, with two tunnels to draw a thorough
#Text= air.
#Text=In Spain they commonly make great opposite windows without glass,
#Text= still shutting those which are next to the sun: so likewise in Turkey and
#Text= Italy (Venice excepted, which brags of her stately glazed palaces) they use
#Text= paper windows to like purpose; and lie, _sub dio_, in the top of their
#Text= flat-roofed houses, so sleeping under the canopy of heaven.
#Text=In some parts
#Text= of [3186]Italy they have windmills, to draw a cooling air out of hollow
#Text= caves, and disperse the same through all the chambers of their palaces, to
#Text= refresh them; as at Costoza, the house of Caesareo Trento, a gentleman of
#Text= Vicenza, and elsewhere.
#Text=Many excellent means are invented to correct nature
#Text= by art.
#Text=If none of these courses help, the best way is to make artificial
#Text= air, which howsoever is profitable and good, still to be made hot and
#Text= moist, and to be seasoned with sweet perfumes, [3187]pleasant and lightsome
#Text= as it may be; to have roses, violets, and sweet-smelling flowers ever in
#Text=sometimes, or sit in a shady seat, must needs be a delectable recreation.
